title: Good Friendship
subtitle: The Entire Spiritual Life
paragraphs: Good evening, everyone. I trust you've had a fruitful day. I do not say happy, though I hope it has been happy.
Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammā sambuddhassa.
Homage to the Buddha, the blessed, noble and fully self-awakened one.

Today we ran a little day retreat for some people, and I think one or two people will be here from that day, from today. One thing that has come out with this lockdown and everything is how people have become neighbourly, helping each other get food and such. It has brought out the friendship which was hidden before.

I thought today might be a good time to look at one or two things the Buddha says about good friendship. This isn't from the Middle Length Sayings; these are taken from the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which is a collection of the discourses by numbers—one of these, two of those, right up to number eleven. There is also a quotation from the Dīgha Nikāya, the Long Discourses, from a discourse to Sīgālaka. It is a discourse devoted to lay people. And there is one here from the Connected Sayings which is about friendship, about good friendship in the spiritual life.

My idea is that I will read out what the Buddha says about good friendship. There are two sides to the question. First of all, we have to bring somebody to mind, or some people to mind, whom we consider to be good, close friends. Of course, your closest friend is, if you're married or in partnership, that would be your closest friend—or your parents or whatever. But just bring certain people to mind, and we're going to ask ourselves, would they? And then afterwards, would I?
The first one is: one should associate with a friend who possesses seven factors.
They give what is hard to give.

The first time round, it's somebody you know—somebody who's a friend. Would they give something that is hard to give? Would they do something for you which was hard to do? In other words, asking a little sacrifice for that.
Would they patiently endure what is hard to endure? In other words, when you're being nasty.
Would they reveal their secrets to you? Would they give confidence like that?
Would you have confidence in them not to tell your secrets to others?
They would not forsake you when you're in trouble.
They would not look down upon you. The word here is despise, but I think that's a bit strong.
Now turning to ourselves: would we? Towards certain people in our lives.
Would we give what is hard to give? Think of an example. It doesn't have to be just one person, but have you actually given what was hard to give?
Have you done what was hard to do?
Have you endured what was unpleasant? Unpleasant about them, that is.
Have you revealed secrets to them that you wouldn't want other people to know? And have you kept confidentiality? Have you preserved their secrets?
Have you ever forsaken somebody who was in trouble? Just not helped them when you could have done?
Have you looked down upon friends on occasion? Or have you indulged that? Occasionally maybe it happens, but have you actually indulged looking down upon them, thinking badly of them?

Now there follows a verse: A friend gives what is hard to give and does what is hard to do. They forgive you your harsh words and endure what is hard to endure. They tell you their secrets and they preserve your secrets. They do not forsake you in difficulties and they do not look down upon you. The person in whom these qualities are found is a friend. One desiring a friend should resort to such a person.
That's the first description of a friend. The next one is similar, of course, but it does have a little twist.
One should associate with a friend who possesses, again, seven qualities.
They are pleasing and agreeable. That's an easy one, isn't it?
They are respected. Somebody who is generally respected. They have to choose if you look around your friendships.
They are a speaker. I tried to find out what exactly that means. I couldn't really find out the meaning and there are no notes on it, so you'll just have to imagine what that means.
Do they patiently endure being spoken to? That's when you have to say something which they don't like but is, from your point of view, for their good.
Do they have deep conversation?
Do they not encourage you to do something which is wrong?
Now what about us? How have we acted in the past?
Have we been pleasing and agreeable?
Can we be respected?
Do we patiently endure being spoken to, corrected?
Do we talk deeply about things, or at least go into things a little bit more than just surface talk?
And do we not lead people into wrongdoing?

So again, this is followed by a verse. They are dear, respected and esteemed, a speaker and one who endures speech. So I presume, not quite sure what that means, to give deep talks and does not enjoin one to do what is wrong. The person here in whom these qualities are found is a friend, benevolent and compassionate. Even if one is dismissed by him, one desiring a friend should resort to such a person.
So even if you meet somebody like that but they don't particularly want to know you, we should try to find somebody similar.
So now there's another way of describing four good friends. Four kinds. This time it's four kinds of good friends and this is the advice he was giving to this man Sīgālaka.
So he says there are four kinds of kind-hearted friends. So again if you can think of somebody:
The friend who is helpful.
A friend who shares one's happiness and suffering.
A friend who points out what is good.
And a friend who's sympathetic.
Now what about ourselves? How do we see ourselves?
Are we helpful?
Do we share our happinesses and sufferings, disappointments and so on?
Do we point to what is good?
Are we sympathetic?
And there are four cases of a helpful friend.
They protect you when you are heedless. Think of somebody who's helped you when you're heedless.
They look after your property when you're heedless. Not necessarily your house or anything, but whatever you've asked them to look after.
Are they a refuge when you're frightened?
And when your need has arisen, have they given twice the wealth required? That's a big much. In other words, have they given more than you asked for?
What about us?
Have we protected someone who was about to be heedless, to do something which would not have looked good?
Have we protected their property if they've been heedless?
Have they been able to take refuge in us when they're frightened, anxious about something?
And when somebody's asked for financial help, have we given them a little bit more?
There are four cases of a friend who shares one's happiness and sufferings. We've come across some of these.
They reveal their secrets to you.
They guard your secrets.
They do not abandon you when you're in trouble.
And this is the big one: they would sacrifice their life for your sake.
Think of anybody who might sacrifice their life for you. It's a tall order, isn't it?
What about us?
Have we shared somebody's happiness and suffering?
Have we not abandoned them when in trouble?
And this final one: is there anyone whom we would sacrifice our life for?

Jesus of course said there is no greater gift than to give one's life for another. And there have of course been cases in history. The one that came to mind was more of a novel, A Tale of Two Cities. Out of love—I can't remember, Darnay is it?—he finally goes to the guillotine replacing this man whom his true love actually loved. She didn't love him. But he was happy to offer his life for her happiness. "It's a far, far better thing I do now than I've ever done before."
Four cases of a friend who points out what is good.
They restrain you from evil. We've had something like that before.
They enjoin you to do what is good. They encourage you to do what is good.
They inform you of what you have not heard. So I presume it's if somebody said something about you, that they're happy to, they will inform you, especially if it's something that might harm you.
And they point to you to the path of heaven. So that, of course, is the ethical path.
There are four cases of a sympathetic friend.
They do not rejoice in your misfortune. Can you think of somebody who does not rejoice in your misfortune?
And they rejoice in your good fortune.
They stop those who dispraise you.
They commend those who speak praise of you.
What about us?
When a friend of ours is born to misfortune, do we rejoice or do we not rejoice? Can you think of an occasion?
Do we rejoice in a friend's good fortune? Or are we caught up in jealousy or envy?
Do you stop somebody who's speaking badly about your friend?
And commend those who speak well of them?
But the final one also is about spiritual friendships.
So here's Ānanda. Ānanda always says that he knows something and then the Buddha always has to correct him.
So here's Ānanda saying, "Bhante, this is half the spiritual life. That is good friendship, good companionship and good comradeship."

So the Buddha says, "No, not so Ānanda, not so. This is the entire spiritual life, Ānanda. That is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. When a person has a good friend, a good companion, a good comrade, it is expected that they will develop and cultivate the Noble Eightfold Path."

So having a good friend on the spiritual path is obviously going to be a great support. I mean, I've known cases where one person within a marriage became a Buddhist and the other one just couldn't stand it really, found it very threatening. It was a very difficult time. I mean, eventually it sorted itself out. But if you happen to be in a relationship where both of you are committed to the path, what you can see, that would be a great support.

The sutta ends by saying it may be understood how the entire spiritual life is good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship. By relying—and then he talks about himself, you see, that confidence that we should have in him—by relying upon me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth; beings subject to old age are freed from aging; beings subject to death are freed from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection and despair are freed from sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection and despair. By this method, Ānanda, it may be understood how the entire spiritual life is good friendship, good companionship and good comradeship.
In other words, when we take refuge in the Buddha and his teaching, they become our very good spiritual companions.

These are just reflections. It's a way that we can use the discourses to consider ourselves and to move us along the path. I can only hope that you are moving along the path and that you will be liberated from all suffering sooner rather than later.
We can begin our practice.
